intro: The Ninth ends with a string hymn in D♭ major, a semitone below the key in which the symphony began. Mahler lets its long phrases break into smaller and smaller pieces, until even a single viola note can hold the room.

sections.label: A · Violins, then a string hymn
sections.mNote: A forceful violin line opens into divided string parts

sections.label: B · High violins, low contrabassoon
sections.mNote: A held A hangs above the rising bass line

sections.label: A′ · Horn and strings recover the hymn
sections.mNote: The two principal tunes intertwine in D♭ major

sections.label: B′ · Held violins and small wind replies
sections.mNote: Strings thin out around fragments of the two tunes

sections.label: Dev · Strings climb against descending lines
sections.mNote: Woodwinds and brass join another long crescendo

sections.label: A″ · The hymn’s last broad statements
sections.mNote: Strings and winds share the returning melody

sections.label: Coda · High violins and cor anglais
sections.mNote: The last wind replies fall among dwindling string phrases

sections.label: Coda · Adagissimo: strings and long rests
sections.mNote: Muted second violins begin the broken final page

cues.title: The violins speak together
cues.text: Both violin sections begin in unison, with a forceful rising leap and falling phrase. Then the other strings enter quietly, dividing into many lines. The little turn that flickered through the Rondo-Burleske has become part of a hymn.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition first-edition score, 1912, p. 164. Lew Smoley describes the opening violin unison, divided strings and connection with the preceding movement: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/listening-guide/listening-guide-movement-4-adagio-sehr-langsam-und-noch-zuruckhaltend/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A bassoon below the hymn
cues.text: The strings leave a D♭ hanging in the violin. From far below, a bassoon climbs slowly towards it. This small, bare passage will keep returning between the hymn’s much fuller statements.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, p. 164; Smoley identifies the held violin D♭ and rising bassoon line between the two principal subjects.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An enormous empty space
cues.text: The violins hold a high A. Contrabassoon and cellos bring back the bassoon’s rising line, far beneath them. The instruments seem separated by an enormous empty space; little violin phrases begin to cross it.
cues.evidence: Smoley describes the first extended interlude: sustained high violin A, contrabassoon and cello ascent, then the violin melody above the low line.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The hymn returns in pieces
cues.text: D♭ major returns. Horn and second violins take part of one tune while first violins and violas carry the other. Their falling phrases and turns fit together, and the quiet beginning soon catches fire.
cues.evidence: Smoley’s guide, return of the principal themes in the tonic and original tempo; it identifies the horn, second violins, first violins and viola combinations.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Walter’s melting cloud
cues.text: In his 1936 book on Mahler, Bruno Walter describes this finale as “like the melting of a cloud in the ethereal blue”. Two years later he conducts the performance playing here, with the Vienna Philharmonic.
cues.evidence: Bruno Walter, Gustav Mahler (1936), quoted in Erik Ryding’s Library of Congress essay, p. 3. The essay also documents the recording of 16 January 1938. https://lcweb2.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/MahlerSymphonyNo9.pdf

cues.title: The strings pull apart
cues.text: The strings press into another long ascent while other lines fall against them. Low woodwinds and brass join the climb. The small turn is everywhere, passed from voice to voice as the orchestra gathers for its great late climax.
cues.evidence: Smoley’s account of the later development describes the second theme in strings, low-woodwind chords, contrary motion and increasing brass participation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The orchestra leaves the strings
cues.text: High violins hold a C♮ above the dwindling orchestra. The cor anglais answers with a falling phrase. Soon only strings remain, passing the tune downwards until the cellos can carry it no further.
cues.evidence: Smoley’s guide, final withdrawal: high violin C♮, cor anglais reply and descending string fragments before the pause.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A page of farewells
cues.text: Adagissimo. Muted second violins begin a small rising phrase, and the remaining strings answer in scraps, with long rests between them. Whole tunes have shrunk to a turn, a falling step, a note held until the next breath.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, p. 180: Adagissimo, muted second violins and fragmented string phrases separated by rests.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The viola’s last turn
cues.text: D♭ major holds at the end. The viola turns its little phrase upwards, where so many earlier turns fell. The chord remains while the notes within it disappear, one by one.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, final bars, p. 180; Smoley identifies the final D♭-major chord and the upward form of the turn in the viola.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: High A, then the low instruments
transitions.from: A · Violins, then a string hymn
transitions.how: The violins leap to a high A and soften to pianissimo. Contrabassoon and cellos begin the rising line previously heard in the bassoon. The upper strings keep fragments of the hymn above this slow ascent.
transitions.evidence: Smoley’s finale guide, first extended interlude: high violin A and returning contrabassoon/cello line.

transitions.title: The horn joins the returning strings
transitions.to: A′ · Horn and strings recover the hymn
transitions.how: Woodwinds repeat falling seconds as the interlude presses forward. D♭ major and the original tempo return. Horn and second violins sing part of the second theme against the first theme in violins and violas.
transitions.evidence: Smoley describes the woodwind bridge and the instrumental combinations at the tonic return.

transitions.title: The violins hold an A♭
transitions.from: A′ · Horn and strings recover the hymn
transitions.to: B′ · Held violins and small wind replies
transitions.how: The climbing violin line reaches a high A♭ and suddenly softens. Oboe and clarinet take fragments of the two tunes while a solo violin keeps the turn. The broad string writing breaks into these small replies.
transitions.evidence: Smoley’s guide describes the high A♭, followed by oboe, clarinet and solo-violin fragments.

transitions.title: The strings gather the scattered phrases
transitions.from: B′ · Held violins and small wind replies
transitions.to: Dev · Strings climb against descending lines
transitions.how: A crescendo on the first theme brings back the second in strongly accented strings. Low woodwinds add chords as the pace quickens. Some lines climb while others descend; horns join them with a broad rising phrase.
transitions.evidence: Smoley’s guide, later development: return of the second theme, low-wind chords, contrary motion and horns.

transitions.title: High C remains above the orchestra
transitions.from: A″ · The hymn’s last broad statements
transitions.to: Coda · High violins and cor anglais
transitions.how: The violins rise to C♮ and hold it as the orchestra withdraws. Woodwinds softly take the hymn’s descending notes; the cor anglais continues with a falling octave. Second violins bring back the rising scale, then the remaining string phrases pass down into the cellos.
transitions.evidence: Smoley’s guide, closing reduction before Adagissimo, including the high C♮, cor anglais octave and descending string phrases.

transitions.title: Muted violins after the pause
transitions.from: Coda · High violins and cor anglais
transitions.to: Coda · Adagissimo: strings and long rests
transitions.how: The cello phrase sinks into silence. At Adagissimo, muted second violins resume the rising scale. Only strings remain, their phrases broken by rests, with the viola’s turn unfolding inside the last D♭-major chords.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, p. 180; Smoley describes the pause, muted second-violin entry and final viola turn.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, first-edition full score (Universal Edition, 1912; Dover reprint)
source.locator: Movement IV, printed pp. 164–180: violin unison and divided-string hymn; bassoon and contrabassoon interludes; strings alone at Adagissimo on p. 180.

timeline.note: Both violin sections play the opening line together before the other strings enter.
The string hymn opens into divided inner parts beneath the first violins.
A bassoon climbs slowly beneath a held violin D♭.
Contrabassoon and cellos rise beneath the violins’ high A.
Horn and strings combine the two principal tunes in D♭ major.
Woodwind replies pass between harp notes, high violins and low strings.
Winds and brass join the strings’ crossing lines in the long crescendo.
A high violin note remains above the last flute and cor anglais replies.
Muted second violins begin the Adagissimo; the remaining strings answer between long rests.
Second violins, violas and cellos remain after first violins and basses fall silent.

fields.note: Commons, the surviving concert-programme catalogue and the Library of Congress essay agree on orchestra and conductor.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The recording sources identify the complete movement but do not establish the performing edition or any local alterations. The 1912 full score is used as a structural reference, not proof of the parts on the 1938 desks.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: 16 January is the documented public concert date. Pristine gives 15–16 January 1938 for its reissue; the inspected evidence does not establish whether any rehearsal material entered the issued matrices. The Commons embedded “1962” digitising tag is not accepted as a performance or transfer date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: The concert-programme catalogue names the hall and city; Commons uses Musikvereinsaal de Vienne.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Commons names only an unspecified audio CD. HMV made the original 78-rpm issue, but the CD label used for this upload has not been identified.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The source CD catalogue number is unknown. Pristine documents the historical ten-disc HMV set as DB 8569–8578; that does not identify the carrier transferred for Commons.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: Pristine lists the original complete-set matrix series 2VH 7027–7046. The inspected DAHR composer listing did not establish a matrix/take match for this digital source; no exhaustive absence is claimed. Specific takes and a verified movement-to-matrix mapping remain unestablished, so the complete-set series is not presented as a side identification for this file.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No engineer for the source CD or Commons transfer is identified. Gaisberg was the original recording producer and Charlie Gregory the recording engineer, not established digital-transfer credits. Andrew Rose’s named 2013 Pristine transfer is a different reissue and is not the source of this Commons upload.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is established. The embedded digitising value 1962 is not corroborated as a transfer date and is not used as one; neither upload nor release dates substitute for it.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Commons supplies an Ogg Vorbis file and an MP3 access derivative.
fields.note: Embedded metadata names Xiph.Org libVorbis I 20100325 (Everywhere). The original 1938 performance was cut on alternating wax-recording machines, but the intervening CD restoration, equalisation, edits and mastering are not identified for this file.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: The underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Mahler died in 1911. This is a term calculation for the composition, not worldwide clearance of an unidentified edition or transfer.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial: Commons applies PD-EU-audio to the sound recording.
fields.note: The inspected template expressly concerns expired performer and producer rights in the European Union. This package is admitted on that territorial recording-rights basis, not merely the composition’s age. United States status is not established; no worldwide public-domain clearance is asserted.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
